title: Trench warfare
description: Land warfare involving static fortification of lines
wiki_lead: Trench warfare is a  type of land warfare using occupied lines largely comprising military trenches, in which combatants are well-protected from the enemy's fire and are substantially sheltered from artillery. Although used in antiquity it fully developed in the 17th century. During the American Civil War (1861–1865), particularly during the sieges of Vicksburg and Petersburg, modern firepower clashed with outdated infantry tactics. Soldiers began digging in to avoid the deadly shelling. This tactical shift signaled the end of classic open-field battles. This development ultimately reached its most extreme and deadly form in World War I (1914–1918). Through the combined use of machine guns, rapid-fire artillery, and barbed wire, the front lines—particularly on the Western Front—became frozen in a kilometer-long, deeply echeloned system of trenches. The trench was now no longer merely a means of siege but, as a defensive infrastructure, determined the entire course of the industrialized war of attrition.
wiki_excerpt:
Trench warfare is a  type of land warfare using occupied lines largely comprising military trenches, in which combatants are well-protected from the enemy's fire and are substantially sheltered from artillery. Although used in antiquity it fully developed in the 17th century. During the American Civil War (1861–1865), particularly during the sieges of Vicksburg and Petersburg, modern firepower clashed with outdated infantry tactics. Soldiers began digging in to avoid the deadly shelling. This tactical shift signaled the end of classic open-field battles. This development ultimately reached its most extreme and deadly form in World War I (1914–1918). Through the combined use of machine guns, rapid-fire artillery, and barbed wire, the front lines—particularly on the Western Front—became frozen in a kilometer-long, deeply echeloned system of trenches. The trench was now no longer merely a means of siege but, as a defensive infrastructure, determined the entire course of the industrialized war of attrition.


Origin
An early mention of the trench dates back to the 5th century B.C. by the Greek historian Thucydides in his work The History of the Peloponnesian War. Here he states: A trench was dug all round the temple and the consecrated ground, and the earth thrown up from the excavation was made to do duty as a wall. [...] Meanwhile the Syracusans marched out and began a second stockade, starting from the city, across the middle of the marsh, digging a trench alongside to make it impossible for the Athenians to carry their wall down to the sea. Furthermore, Aristotle, in Nicomachean Ethics, states that "generals" drew their soldiers in front of the trenches.
A more general use of trenches can be found in the accounts of Roman historians. Among them are Polybius who refers to trenches several times in his work about the Punic wars and Flavius Josephus mentioning the use of trenches during the First Jewish-Roman War. The most comprehensive report comes from Caesar. In De Bello Gallico he describes in detail the construction of trenches during the Siege of Alesia. In order to protect the soldiers working on the main siege constructions a 20 feet wide trench was dug. Additionally two further inner trenches each 15 feet broad and 15 feet deep were dug and flooded.
Until the early modern period, trenches served primarily as obstacles e.g., by filling them with water, against enemy attacks. In the 17th century the Ottomans had developed a system of parallels and saps(trenches running zigzag towards the enemy). Placing all the infantry into those trenches, this system would've given the besiegers protection against the enemy artillery. Although there had been earlier examples of trench parallels in western Europe, in the second half of the 17th century the French military engineer Sébastien Le Prestre de Vauban adopted this successful system. His system envisioned three parallel trenches that were connected via zig-zagging approach trenches. The trenches usually measured four to five feet in depth and six to twelve feet in width. Gabions were fitted to the front of the trench parallels serving as the trenches' parapets. Sometimes ledges were added to the parallels as firing platforms for the infantry assigned to the trenches. The sloping rear sides of the parallels made sure that the besieging troops could retreat in the event of a garrison sortie. Lodgements as well as redoubts were constructed to serve as assembly points and to house troops and workers.


American Civil War
During the American Civil War, particularly during the Overland and Petersburg campaigns, an early form of trench warfare, which would come to define World War I, developed. grok_lead: Trench warfare is a type of land warfare in which opposing armies construct and occupy extensive networks of trenches as defensive fortifications to shield against enemy artillery and small arms fire, resulting in prolonged stalemates characterized by static positions and high casualties. This form of combat became synonymous with World War I (1914â1918), particularly on the Western Front, where it emerged after the initial phase of mobile warfare ground to a halt in late 1914 due to the devastating effectiveness of machine guns and heavy artillery. The trenches stretched approximately 475 miles from the North Sea to the Swiss border, forming a complex system that included front-line fire trenches, support lines, and reserve positions connected by communication trenches, all reinforced with sandbags, barbed wire, and wooden revetments. Life in the trenches was marked by appalling conditions that exacerbated the physical and psychological toll of combat. Soldiers endured constant exposure to mud, water, and filth, which led to widespread diseases such as trench footâa condition caused by prolonged exposure to cold, wet conditions that could lead to severe tissue damage and often required amputation âand dysentery, while infestations of rats and lice added to the misery. Daily routines involved nighttime patrols and repairs under cover of darkness to avoid detection, with daytime spent in cramped dugouts prone to collapse from shelling; mental strain from incessant artillery barrages contributed to "shell shock," an early recognition of what is now known as post-traumatic stress disorder. Rations were basic, typically consisting of hard biscuits, canned meat, and occasional jam, though supply disruptions were common. Tactically, trench warfare relied on massive artillery bombardments to soften enemy lines before infantry assaults across the exposed "no-man's land"âa barren, cratered zone between opposing trenches that claimed millions of lives. Machine guns, rifles, and later chemical weapons like mustard gas dominated defenses, making advances extraordinarily costly; for instance, the first day of the Battle of the Somme in 1916 resulted in over 57,000 British casualties. Though trenches had been used in earlier conflicts like the American Civil War, their scale and duration in World War I set them apart, influencing military doctrine and leading to innovations such as tanks that eventually broke the deadlock in 1918. The overall impact included estimates of over 10 million military deaths, with trench systems totaling around 25,000 miles across all fronts, underscoring the human cost of industrialized warfare.
